rules: Inverse variance works with every metric, both models, and both arm-level and precomputed data.
A precomputed estimate can only be pooled by methods that take an estimate and its variance: inverse variance, bayesmeta, rma.mv.
Mantel-Haenszel needs arm-level counts and gives OR, RR, RD (2x2 tables) or IRR, IRD (person-time). Common effect only.
"Random-effects Mantel-Haenszel" is not a separate method: the random-effects estimate uses inverse-variance weights.
Peto needs 2x2 tables and gives only the Peto odds ratio. Common effect only. For rare events, balanced arms, small effects.
GLMM gives OR (2x2), IRR (two-group counts), logit proportion and log rate. RR and RD are experimental.
v11 wrong: lists OR, RR, RD
GLMM random effects uses maximum likelihood only.
v11 wrong: says REML, ML, EB
GLMM does not apply to continuous outcomes.
For rare events avoid inverse variance, including DerSimonian-Laird.
Subgroup analysis and meta-regression need moderators: available in rma.uni, rma.glmm, rma.mv and bayesmeta (bmr); not in rma.mh or rma.peto.
agrees; answers v11's open question on bayesmeta
Cumulative and leave-one-out functions exist for rma.uni, rma.mh and rma.peto only.
v11 wrong for GLMM and rma.mv
Cumulative and leave-one-out need a model without moderators.
bayesmeta has no cumulative or leave-one-out function: none is in its manual's index. It computes the posterior numerically (a grid approximation and the DIRECT algorithm).
Hartung-Knapp intervals apply to rma.uni random-effects models only.
REML is the default in metafor and RevMan. Cochrane also cites Paule-Mandel and says no estimator is universally preferable.
v11 overstates: calls REML Cochrane's preference
Network meta-analysis can use a common-effect or a random-effects model. Chapter 11 never mentions excluding the common-effect model; netmeta and the rma.mv example fit both.
P-score and SUCRA are rankings computed after a network model is fitted. They are outputs, not effect measures.
v11 wrong: lists them as metrics
A network analysis must check transitivity and consistency (node-splitting, design decomposition, net heat plot).
Networks usually assume one common between-study variance across comparisons.
Mantel-Haenszel for networks (netmetabin) is common-effect only.
IPD: two-stage analysis joins the precomputed pathway. One-stage analysis needs a mixed-effects regression stratified by study.
Cluster-randomized trial: divide the sample size (and events) by the design effect 1 + (M - 1) x ICC, or multiply the SE by its square root.
Crossover trial: use a paired analysis; without paired data, impute the SD of differences from an assumed correlation.
v11 wrong: applies the cluster formula

Study with three or more arms in a pairwise analysis: combine arms (recommended in most situations), model the correlation, or use a network. Choosing one pair, or splitting the shared group, is not generally recommended.
Time-to-event from O - E and V: Cochrane notes that RevMan offers fixed-effect methods only, and this map follows it; log hazard ratios with SEs are pooled by inverse variance.
Diagnostic accuracy: sensitivity and specificity are pooled jointly (bivariate model); the HSROC model is equivalent without covariates.
Prediction model performance: pool the c-statistic on the logit scale and O:E on the log scale, random effects with Hartung-Knapp and a prediction interval.
Tests for funnel plot asymmetry need at least 10 studies; Egger's original test is not recommended for odds ratios or SMDs.
Trim and fill and selection models work on rma.uni models only (trim and fill: no moderators).
Meta-regression is generally not advised with fewer than ten studies.

A network's standardized mean difference is Cohen's d. From arm-level data, pairwise() computes it that way for netmeta, since the small-sample correction of Hedges' g would make a multi-arm study's comparisons disagree; contrast-level estimates should be Cohen's d for the same reason. The map offers one network SMD.
v11 wrong: offers d and g separately for rma.mv and gemtc networks

In this map, the Peto odds ratio is offered only with Peto's method. Cochrane presents it as the estimate Peto's method computes: an approximate log odds ratio from observed minus expected events and their variance. escalc(measure="PETO") also computes it study by study; this map doesn't offer pooling it with another method.

gemtc's network models take the odds ratio, the risk ratio, the mean difference, the standardized mean difference and, from events and exposure, a rate ratio (which gemtc labels a hazard ratio). It has no likelihood for the risk difference, arcsine difference, ratio of means or rate difference.
v11 wrong: offers every network measure for gemtc
cross_cutting: standard, subgroup, meta-regression, cumulative, leave-one-out, sensitivity. What each method supports is listed on the method.
Between-study variance, I-squared, Q test, prediction interval (encouraged with about five or more studies).
Funnel plot, regression test (regtest), trim and fill (trimfill), selection models (selmodel).
Cluster trials, crossover trials, studies with several arms, repeated measurements.
Ranking (P-score, SUCRA, rankogram), league table, consistency checks.

open_items: Read the Cochrane diagnostic accuracy handbook, Ch. 9 and 10 (needs a Cochrane account) and confirm the diagnostic branch.
Read Riley et al. 2019 and Debray et al. 2017 in full and confirm the prognosis branch.
Confirm the R package for one-stage IPD, pairwise (network: multinma, #59).
Confirm how gemtc reads contrast-level data (the scale of diff, and its likelihood).
Confirm from metafor's and gemtc's documentation how their networks take a standardized mean difference (Cohen's d, R31).

unconfirmed.why: R31's source covers netmeta; how rma.mv networks take an SMD is still to read in metafor's documentation
gemtc fits an SMD (normal/smd likelihood), but its help page doesn't say whether it is Cohen's d (R31)
multinma's survival likelihoods include accelerated failure time models, which give time ratios; its help page doesn't say which give a hazard ratio (#59)

unconfirmed_input.why: gemtc takes contrast-level data as diff and std.err, but its help pages don't say what scale diff is on or how it is matched to a likelihood (issue #40)

IV.label: Inverse variance
IV.note: Random effects: 12 estimators of the between-study variance (REML is the default); Hartung-Knapp interval available (test="knha"). Cumulative and leave-one-out need a model without moderators.

MH.label: Mantel-Haenszel
MH.note: No moderators. Generally preferred to inverse variance for common-effect binary analyses (Cochrane 10.4.1).

PETO.label: Peto
PETO.note: For rare events, balanced arms and small effects. Not a default (Cochrane 10.4.2).

GLMM.label: Generalized linear mixed model
GLMM.note: Common effect is method="EE"; random effects uses maximum likelihood only. RR and RD are experimental. No cumulative or leave-one-out function.

LRP.label: Penalised logistic regression (rare events)
LRP.note: Handles single and double zero studies without a continuity correction. Reports a common-effect and a random-effects result; the random-effects one uses a multiplicative heterogeneity parameter (phi), not a between-study variance.

BAYES.label: Bayesian normal-normal hierarchical model
BAYES.note: Computes the posterior numerically: a grid approximation for the heterogeneity and the DIRECT algorithm for the effect. Meta-regression and subgroups through bmr(). No cumulative or leave-one-out function found in the manual.

MV.label: Multilevel / multivariate
MV.note: For studies that contribute several dependent estimates. Without a random term it fits a fixed-effects model (v11 says random only). REML or ML. No Hartung-Knapp, cumulative or leave-one-out function.

OEV.label: Observed minus expected and variance (log-rank / Peto)
OEV.fn: metafor::rma.uni(yi = (O - E) / V, vi = 1 / V, method = "EE")
OEV.note: Cochrane 6.8.2: each study's log hazard ratio is (O - E)/V, with standard error 1/sqrt(V). Pooled with inverse-variance weights in metafor's equal-effects model. Cochrane 10.9: only fixed-effect methods in RevMan.

IPD1.label: One-stage regression on participant data (pairwise)
IPD1.note: Stratify by study (Cochrane 26.4.2, 26.4.5). R packages still to confirm.

NM_GT.label: Frequentist, graph-theoretical
NM_GT.note: Arm-level data go through pairwise(). Between-study variance: DL, REML or ML. Does not support meta-regression.

NM_MV.label: Frequentist, multivariate
NM_MV.note: Arm-based or contrast-based. The documented example fits both a fixed-effects and a random-effects network model.

NM_MH.label: Mantel-Haenszel for networks (sparse binary data)
NM_MH.note: Methods MH and NCH are common-effect only.

NM_BAYES.label: Bayesian hierarchical (MCMC)
NM_BAYES.note: Supports meta-regression. linearModel="fixed" fits a fixed-effect model. Its likelihoods give the odds ratio, risk ratio, mean difference and standardized mean difference; from events and exposure, its Poisson model gives a rate ratio, which gemtc labels a hazard ratio. Contrast-level input is to check.

NM_IPD.label: One-stage regression on participant data (network)
NM_IPD.note: A Bayesian model fitted in Stan, with fixed or random treatment effects and regression on covariates. Its likelihoods include Bernoulli (logit) for binary outcomes, normal (identity) for continuous ones and survival models for time-to-event data; which survival likelihoods give a hazard ratio is to check (#59).

BIV.label: Bivariate model (Reitsma)
BIV.note: Estimation: reml (default), ml, mm, vc, or fixed. Equivalent to the HSROC model when there are no covariates.

HSROC.label: Hierarchical summary ROC model (Rutter and Gatsonis)
HSROC.note: Fits random effects for each study's accuracy and threshold from its 2x2 counts, so the threshold can vary between studies. fitRutterGatsonisSubgroup() takes one study-level subgroup and fitRutterGatsonisReg() study-level covariates.

DTA_UNI.label: Univariate pooling
DTA_UNI.note: Ignores the correlation between sensitivity and specificity.

VAL.label: Meta-analysis of prediction model performance
VAL.note: REML by default, Hartung-Knapp interval, prediction interval; Bayesian option.

DR.label: Dose-response meta-analysis
DR.note: One-stage or two-stage. Covariance by Greenland-Longnecker or Hamling. Linear or non-linear trend.
